messages.subject: how to separate X chromosome
messages.body_plain:

But I don't know the way to separate it while still recognizing X chr.

messages.subject: Re: how to separate X chromosome
messages.body_plain:
If you use movemarker() to move some of the X chromosome markers to a new chromosome, that new chromosome will also have class "X" and so treated as another X chromosome.
Here's an example:

data(hyper)
mapX <- pull.map(hyper, chr="X")[[1]]
for(i in 3:length(mapX)) {
    hyper <- movemarker(hyper, names(mapX)[i], "Xb", mapX[i])
}
summary(hyper)

It'll give a warning about having more than one X chromosome; I'm not totally sure that everything will work.

Alternatively, if you have a chromosome that's being treated like an autosome and you want it to be treated like an X chromosome, you can assign it class "X" like this:

    class(hyper$geno[["Xb"]]) <- "X"

karl

messages.subject: Rqtl2 vs Rqtl
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm new to using Rqtl2 for initial QTL mapping analysis (Interval Mapping) and I'm looking for guidance on how to perform MQM. While I found multiple functions for MQM in Rqtl, my main reason for using an R package for QTL mapping is to overcome computational limits of older Windows Interface software. Rqtl2 offers the 'cores =' argument in key functions, which is crucial for handling larger datasets efficiently. But on the other hand I'm still not able to find MQM functions, or how to conduct it in its tutorials.

As a beginner, I came here to seek help:

Which package version should I use? I believe Rqtl2 is the right choice since I'm working with high-density data.

How can I perform MQM using Rqtl2?

Thank you for your assistance.

Best regards,"

Othmane

messages.subject: Re: Rqtl2 vs Rqtl
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl2 handle more types of crosses. If you are working with multi-parent populations like MAGIC lines, Collaborative Cross, heterogeneous stock, diversity outbred mice, you will need to use R/qtl2.
But if you are focusing on a traditional two-parent cross such as a backcross or intercross, either R/qtl1 or R/qtl2 may work for you.

R/qtl2 includes fit of linear mixed models to account for population structure. So if you want to use a LMM to account for varying relationships, you'll need to use R/qtl2.

But R/qtl1 has many multiple-QTL model methods, including the MQM approach you mentioned, and these have not yet been implemented in R/qtl2. So if you're using a two-parent cross and want to use MQM, you should stick with R/qtl1.

karl

messages.subject: Coverting physical location (bp) to Mbp
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am working with rice genotyping by sequencing data that gives position in basepairs. I have over 93,000 markers so it is very dense and I believe I can convert into mbp and it will be accepted by the program. Is there any function that can do this conversion easily? Converting all 93,944 markers from bp to mbp will not be a small task.

I would rather avoid making an assumption on recombination rates etc.. for the conversion of bp to cM which I know some have assumed this rate is ~273kb per cM in rice.

Thank you for any input!
Rachel Tavares

messages.subject: Re: Coverting physical location (bp) to Mbp
messages.body_plain:
You can load it into R/qtl with positions in basepairs, and it will give a warning, but there shouldn't be an error that will prevent you from working with the data.

You can then use the function rescalemap() to rescale the positions from basepairs to Mbp, or to rescale them to estimated cM.
Scaling 273 kbp per cM means scaling 1 Mbp to (1/0.273) cM

mycross_Mbp <- rescalemap(mycross_bp, scale=1e-6)
mycross_cM <- rescalemap(mycross_Mbp, scale=1/0.273)

karl

messages.subject: Re: Removing individual missing nearly all marker data
messages.subject_clean: Removing individual missing nearly all marker data
messages.body_plain:
Could you show the code you used, and the error?

One way to drop the individuals with the most missing data is using nmissing() to count the number of missing genotypes for each individual. Here's an example.

library(qtl)
data(hyper)
nmis <- nmissing(hyper)
hypersub <- subset(hyper, ind= (nmis < max(nmis)) )

nind(hyper) # 250
nind(hypersub) # 240  (10 individuals missing exactly 133 markers)

karl

messages.subject: Re: Removing individual missing nearly all marker data
messages.subject_clean: Removing individual missing nearly all marker data
messages.body_plain:
match() in this case is going to return a single value, and then is.na <http://is.na>(match( ) ) is going to be either TRUE or FALSE, according to whether "CD174_1" is found within mycross$pheno$id.
The ind argument in the subset.cross() function needs either a numeric index or a vector of TRUE/FALSE with length being the number of individuals.

I think this might work:

ind2drop <- c("CD174_1")

mycross <- subset(mycross, ind= -match(ind2drop, mycross$pheno$id))

That is, use match() to get the numeric index and then make it negative to take all the others but not this one.

karl

messages.subject: Re: Removing alternative alleles not found in parent samples
messages.subject_clean: Removing alternative alleles not found in parent samples
messages.body_plain:
I’m not sure I understand the context, as in R/qtl1, the genotypes have to be coded like A/H/B where one parent has the A allele and the other parent has the B allele.

But you could pull out the genotypes as a matrix with pull.geno, find the columns where the two parents have matching genotypes, and then use drop.markers to omit those markers.

karl
